title: Sandbox: the minimum of every window
lead: A sandbox page, AI-written and not part of the book. The same lesson shape as 99.1 on a harder case, where what the obvious way wastes is less plain to see.
notes: A trial page: nothing here is the book's.

exercises.prompt: The window holds 7, 3, 9, 4, 6, in that order, and slides right. Which of these numbers can never be the minimum of this window or a later one?

options: 3, since it is the minimum already
answer.solution: 7 has 3 to its right and 9 has 4: each is beaten by a smaller number that stays in the window longer. 3, 4 and 6 have nothing smaller to their right, so each may be the minimum once the ones before it have left.

exercises.prompt: The numbers arrive in increasing order, so no number is ever struck out. How many comparisons does the fast way make for $n$ numbers?

options: About $n$: one for each number that arrives
About $nk$: the queue holds $k$ numbers and each arrival is compared with all of them
answer.solution: An arriving number is compared with the back of the queue only. The comparison fails at once, since the back is smaller, and the number joins. The queue is never scanned.

exercises.prompt: Which of these problems gives way to the same insight, that a candidate beaten by a newer one can be dropped for good?

options: For each day's temperature, how many days until a warmer one
Whether a sorted array holds two numbers with a given sum
The sum of every window of $k$ numbers
Whether a string of brackets is balanced
answer.solution: Keep the days still waiting for a warmer one. A new day settles every waiting day that is colder, and those never need looking at again. The sum of a window needs a different insight (neighbouring windows share most of their numbers), and the other two need neither.
